title: FDA Suspends Mumbai Eatery's Licence After Diner Allegedly Finds Rat in Dosa
excerpt: Radhakrishna Hotel in Borivali West lost its food licence after a customer said he found a dead rat in his Mysore masala dosa — the latest flashpoint in FDA chief Tukaram Mundhe's festive-season crackdown.
body:
• The Maharashtra FDA has suspended the food licence of Radhakrishna Hotel in Borivali West after a customer, Amit Trivedi, alleged he found a dead rat in his Mysore masala dosa — reportedly after taking a few bites, which left him vomiting. The restaurant's licence is suspended pending investigation.
  • Trivedi, who was dining with his two brothers and son, reported the incident to the local police; Senior Police Inspector Pushpalata Mandale confirmed the complaint was referred to the FDA, which then acted against the hotel.
  • The case has become tangled in politics: Shiv Sena (UBT) MP Sanjay Raut alleged FDA officials demanded bribes worth lakhs to withdraw closure notices or restore suspended licences. FDA Commissioner Tukaram Mundhe rejected the charge, asserting zero tolerance for corruption while demanding concrete evidence.
  • Reader utility: if you find a foreign object in restaurant food, photograph it immediately and report it to the restaurant, the local police and the FDA — that chain is exactly what moved this complaint from a dining table to a licence suspension within days.

The news

A family dinner at a Borivali West eatery has turned into one of Mumbai's ugliest food-safety flashpoints this year. The Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration has suspended the licence of Radhakrishna Hotel after diner Amit Trivedi alleged he discovered a dead rat inside his Mysore masala dosa — after he had already eaten a few bites, an experience that reportedly left him vomiting in distress.

Trivedi, who was at the restaurant with his two brothers and son for South Indian food, contacted the local police over the discovery. Senior Police Inspector Pushpalata Mandale confirmed the complaint was subsequently referred to the FDA, which suspended the hotel's licence and launched an investigation, according to The CSR Journal.

On the same day the incident surfaced, the FDA also moved against Kyani & Co., the 122-year-old Irani café. A surprise inspection led personally by FDA Commissioner Tukaram Mundhe on September 27 found rat droppings, live flies and dead cockroaches on the premises, blood accumulating in a refrigerator and an open sewage manhole in the food-processing area. Its FSSAI licence was suspended under the agency's "Safe Food, Safe Maharashtra" drive.

Context & background

The suspensions are the sharp end of a festive-season enforcement campaign that ran from September 23 to 27. In those five days, the FDA suspended 30 food establishments across Maharashtra — 13 in Mumbai, six in the Konkan region, eight in the Pune division and three in Sambhajinagar — and seized roughly 50.6 tonnes of food items, including sweets, milk products and edible oils, worth an estimated ₹1.19 crore. Inspectors also confiscated banned products valued at ₹30.93 lakh, registered 22 FIRs, arrested 30 people, sealed three establishments and seized three distribution vehicles.

Mumbai's restaurant belt has been under the scanner for weeks. In August, the FDA suspended Hotel Radha in Malad West after inspectors found rats — one entering the kitchen through an open drainage line — and cockroaches on a dough-mixing machine, acting under Section 32(3) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. A day later, Janta Tawa & Grill in Kurla West lost its licence over unsafe raw-meat storage. Popular eateries including Shalimar, Noor Mohammadi and Rahmaniya have also faced suspension for pest infestations and hygiene lapses, India Today reported.

The crackdown has now drawn a political counterattack. Raut alleged that enforcement officials were demanding bribes from businesses facing action — payments to withdraw closure notices or restore suspended licences. Mundhe pushed back, saying he has zero tolerance for corruption but that action against any official requires concrete evidence.

Impact & analysis

Two things are true at once here. The FDA's drive is arguably the most aggressive restaurant-hygiene enforcement Mumbai has seen in years — 30 suspensions in five days sends a message no restaurateur can ignore, and the seizures show the problem extends well beyond kitchens into supply chains. But Raut's bribery allegation, whether proven or not, points to the perennial risk of such drives: when inspectors hold the power to shut a business overnight, the line between enforcement and extortion needs independent oversight.

For diners, the episode is a reminder that celebrated names are no shield. A 122-year-old Irani café with a loyal following failed the same basic tests — pest control, drainage, refrigeration — as a suburban dosa joint. Reputation, in other words, is not a food-safety certificate.

What's next

The investigation into Radhakrishna Hotel will determine what happened and whether further action — including prosecution under the Food Safety and Standards Act — follows. The restaurant stays shut until its licence is restored. With the festive season still underway, Mundhe's teams are expected to keep raiding; whether Raut's corruption charges produce evidence or evaporate will decide if the crackdown keeps its moral authority.
nri_angle: Mumbai's restaurant scene is a pilgrimage stop for visiting NRIs; the crackdown is a reminder that even beloved legacy eateries can fail basic hygiene checks, so diners should trust FSSAI compliance over reputation.
author: Diaspora Desk
